versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 13 In Noah’s six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. So Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. 14 By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry.

15 Then God said to Noah, 16 “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives. 17 Bring out all the living creatures that are with you—birds, livestock, and everything that crawls upon the ground—so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it.”

18 So Noah came out, along with his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives. 19 Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird—everything that moves upon the earth—came out of the ark, kind by kind.

context_lines: Noah sees that the surface is drying before the family leaves. The account distinguishes what he observes in the first month from the dry earth and God's command in the second. His departure follows God's word, just as his entrance did. Preservation in the ark leads to a new responsibility outside it.

God names the whole household and the creatures that are to come out. The purpose is life spreading again: the animals are to breed and multiply on the earth. The closing description of creatures leaving in their groups echoes their ordered entrance. The focus is not merely that Noah has survived, but that the life entrusted to him is released into the world.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as an obedient departure and a renewed beginning for humanity and the other creatures. [Wesley's introduction to chapter 8 and notes on verses 13–14](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) distinguish the appearance of drying ground from its readiness for habitation, while the narrative itself makes God's command the immediate basis for leaving.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The call for living creatures to multiply recalls the blessings of [Genesis 1:22, 28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/genesis/1.htm). This is a supported parallel with creation: God preserves life through judgment and again directs it to fill the earth. Noah's release is part of that purpose for the world, not simply the end of an individual ordeal.

The renewed beginning is not yet the final freedom of creation. The next chapter still contains sin and death, while [Romans 8:19–23](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/8.htm) looks toward creation's release from decay along with the redemption of God's children. What God preserves here continues toward a restoration greater than life immediately after the flood.
